units.title: Saying what something is
units.goal: Point at a thing or a person and say what it is.
explain: Korean has no word for is. Instead the ending 이에요 or 예요 is glued onto the end of the noun itself, and that ending carries the whole meaning of it is.

Which one you use depends on the last letter of the noun. If the noun ends in a consonant, use 이에요. If it ends in a vowel, use 예요. That is the entire rule, and you will meet the same consonant-or-vowel question in almost every ending in this course, so it is worth getting comfortable with now.
The sentence needs no other words. 학생이에요 on its own is a complete Korean sentence.
notes: To ask a question, change nothing but your voice — 학생이에요? with the tone rising. Korean does not reorder the sentence for questions.
The negative is a separate word: 아니에요. 저는 학생이 아니에요 — I am not a student. Notice the noun takes 이/가 in front of 아니에요.

exercises.qEn: I'm an office worker. (회사원 ends in ㄴ)
exercises.why: 회사원 ends in a consonant, so 이에요.
커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ, so 예요.
The negative of 이에요/예요 is the separate word 아니에요, and the noun in front takes 가.

pairs.aEn: student — just the word, on its own
pairs.note: Nothing was added but the ending, and a bare noun became a whole sentence. Korean needs no separate word for is.
친구 ends in the vowel ㅜ, so it can only take 예요. The consonant-or-vowel question decides almost every ending in this course.
Not one word moved. A question is the same sentence with your voice rising at the end.
The negative is not a new ending but a separate word, 아니에요. The noun in front of it takes 이 (or 가 after a vowel).

units.title: Marking what the sentence is about
units.goal: Introduce yourself, and compare one thing against another.
explain: 은/는 is stuck onto a noun to announce as for this — it sets up what the rest of the sentence is going to talk about. 저는 means as for me.
Consonant ending takes 은, vowel ending takes 는. Same question as the last unit.

It does two jobs at once, and the second one surprises people. Besides naming the topic, 은/는 quietly sets that topic against something else. 김치는 매워요 does not only say kimchi is spicy — it hints kimchi, unlike the other thing we were discussing. Koreans hear that contrast even when nobody says it out loud, which is why 저는 sounds natural at the start of a conversation and slightly pointed in the middle of one.

examples.ko: 저는 베트남 사람이에요. 친구는 네팔 사람이에요.
examples.rom: jeoneun Beteunam saramieyo. chinguneun Nepal saramieyo.
examples.en: I'm Vietnamese. My friend is Nepali.

notes: 저 is the humble I, used with anyone senior to you or anyone you have just met. 나 is the casual one, for close friends. At work, use 저.
Korean drops the topic the moment it is obvious. After 저는 한국에 왔어요, the next five sentences will have no 저 in them at all. Repeating it sounds like you are insisting.

exercises.why: 이름 ends in the consonant ㅁ, so 은.
저 ends in a vowel, so 는.

exercises.q: Which one would a worker use to introduce themselves to a manager?
exercises.why: 저 is the humble form. 나 is for friends your own age or younger.

pairs.bEn: Coffee I do like… (but something else, not so much)
pairs.note: 는 does not mean anything you can translate. It lifts 커피 out and sets it against something unsaid — you can hear the but coming.
Both are correct. 는 announces what the sentence is about, which matters most when you are answering a question about someone else.

pairs.aEn: This is the team leader. (the answer to who is it?)
pairs.bEn: This person is the team leader. (introducing them)
pairs.note: 이/가 points: this one, not someone else. 은/는 takes a person already in front of you and says something about them.
이름 ends in the consonant ㅁ, so it takes 은. 는 is only for a noun ending in a vowel, like 저는.

units.title: Saying something exists, or does not
units.goal: Say what you have, what is here, and what is missing.
explain: 있어요 covers both there is and I have. 없어요 is its opposite — there is none, I do not have it. Korean uses one pair of words where English uses two.
The thing that exists is marked with 이/가: consonant ending takes 이, vowel ending takes 가.
You will use 없어요 constantly. It is the honest answer to most questions in your first month — 시간 없어요, 돈 없어요, 잘 모르겠어요.

head: Meaning
Word
Example
rows: there is not / I don't have
시간 없어요 — I don't have time

examples.en: I don't have money right now.
There are a lot of people here.

notes: In speech the particle 이/가 is often dropped: 시간 있어요? is what you will actually hear. Write it, but do not be confused when it goes missing.
맛있어요 (delicious) and 재미있어요 (fun) are 있어요 hiding inside a longer word — literally has taste and has interest. Their opposites are 맛없어요 and 재미없어요.

exercises.why: 돈 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so 이.

options: There's a lot of work today.

pairs.note: These are two different words, not one word negated. There is no 안 있어요 — you must learn 없다 as its own verb.
있다 covers both there is and I have. Which one it means comes from the rest of the sentence, not from the verb.

pairs.bEn: Got time? — the same question, the way it is usually said.
pairs.note: In speech 이/가 is often left out and the meaning does not change. Expect to hear it missing.
없어요 says there is none. 아니에요 says it is not that thing. Both come out as not in English, which is why they get swapped.

units.title: The everyday verb ending
units.goal: Say what you do, using the ending that covers almost every conversation you will have.
explain: Every Korean verb in the dictionary ends in 다: 가다 to go, 먹다 to eat, 일하다 to work. You never say the 다 form out loud. You cut it off and add an ending, and the polite everyday ending is 아요 or 어요.

Look at the last vowel of the stem. If it is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아요. Anything else takes 어요. Verbs ending in 하다 are irregular and become 해요 — and there are hundreds of them, so learning 해요 alone buys you a lot.
This one ending covers the present and the near future at once. 가요 is I go, I am going and I will go in a minute. Korean lets context do that work.

examples.en: I go at seven in the morning.
Have you had lunch? I'm eating now.

notes: Some stems squash together when the ending is added: 보 + 아요 becomes 봐요, 마시 + 어요 becomes 마셔요, 주 + 어요 becomes 줘요. Say them out loud and the reason is obvious — the short way is easier to pronounce.
Drop the 요 and you have the casual form used with close friends: 가, 먹어, 해. At work, keep the 요 on. It costs one syllable and it is the difference between sounding polite and sounding blunt.

exercises.why: The stem vowel ㅓ is not ㅏ or ㅗ, so 어요.

pairs.note: The dictionary form is what you look up; it is not what you say. Every verb you meet has to be turned into 아요/어요 before it leaves your mouth.
먹 has the vowel ㅓ, so 어요. 하다 is irregular and becomes 해요 — it is the one you will say most, so learn it as its own word.
The verb did not change. 아요/어요 covers now and the near future, and the time word tells you which.

pairs.bEn: See you tomorrow. (to a close friend)
pairs.note: Drop the 요 and the sentence becomes casual. Same meaning, but at work keep the 요.

units.title: Where things happen, and where they are
units.goal: Tell someone where you are going and where you work — and stop mixing the two up.
explain: 에 marks a destination or a fixed location: 회사에 가요 I go to the company, 집에 있어요 I am at home. It also marks a time: 일곱 시에 at seven o'clock.
에서 marks where an action happens: 공장에서 일해요 I work at the factory. If something is being done there, use 에서.
The test is the verb. 가다, 오다, 있다 and 없다 take 에. Almost everything else — 일하다, 먹다, 만나다, 사다 — takes 에서. 에서 also means from: 베트남에서 왔어요 I came from Vietnam.

examples.en: I go to the company at eight.
I eat lunch at the canteen.

notes: 어디에 있어요? asks where something is. 어디에서 일해요? asks where you do something. Both are common and they are not interchangeable.
에서 is often shortened to 서 in speech: 어디서 왔어요?

exercises.why: 일하다 is an action done at a place, so 에서.

exercises.qEn: I go to the company at eight.
exercises.why: A clock time takes 에, and 가다 takes 에.

pairs.note: 에 marks where something simply IS. 에서 marks where something HAPPENS. One letter of difference, and putting it the wrong way round is the commonest mistake at this level.
Going TO a place is 에. Doing something AT a place is 에서.
에서 is where the call comes from. 에 is where it goes to. Same verb, and the particle alone turns it round.

pairs.aEn: I eat lunch at the canteen.
pairs.note: English says at for both, but eating is something you do there, so it needs 에서. Keep 에 for 가다, 오다, 있다 and 없다.

units.title: The two sets of numbers
units.form: 하나 둘 셋 / 일 이 삼
units.goal: Say a time, a price and a phone number without freezing.
explain: Korean has two complete number systems and you need both. The native set — 하나, 둘, 셋 — counts things and gives the hour. The Chinese-derived set — 일, 이, 삼 — gives minutes, money, dates, phone numbers and anything above ninety-nine.
The clock uses both at once, and this trips up everyone: 세 시 삼십 분 is three thirty. Native for the hour, Sino for the minutes. There is no way around it.
Money is always Sino, and it is counted in units of ten thousand: 만 원 is 10,000 won, 십만 원 is 100,000, 백만 원 is a million. A monthly wage is usually said in 만 — 이백오십만 원 is 2,500,000 won.

examples.ko: 지금 몇 시예요? 두 시 십 분이에요.
examples.rom: jigeum myeot siyeyo? du si sip bunieyo.
examples.en: What time is it? It's ten past two.

notes: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 shorten before a counter: 한 개, 두 시, 세 명, 네 번. Never 하나 개.
In a phone number, zero is 공 and the dash is said 에. Koreans say the digits one at a time.
몇 means how many and pairs with a counter: 몇 시 what time, 몇 명 how many people, 몇 개 how many pieces.

exercises.why: Hours use the native set, and 셋 shortens to 세 before 시.
Minutes use the Sino set: 삼십 분.

exercises.q: How is 010 said in a phone number?
exercises.why: Zero in a phone number is 공, and each digit is said separately.

pairs.note: Same number, two systems. Hours take the native set, floors take the Sino set. There is no rule you can reason out — it is learned per counter.
A clock time uses both in one breath: native for the hour, Sino for the minutes. Age goes back to native.
Before a counter, 하나 둘 셋 넷 shorten to 한 두 세 네. 두 개, never 둘 개.
시 is the hour on the clock, 시간 is a length of time. Both use the native 세. The ending changes only because 시간 ends in a consonant.
